subtopic: DESIGNATION OF SPECIAL AREAS-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
That being so, perhaps the House will be disposed to demonstrate to this son of Ireland that charity which Irishmen the world over are noted for. With the unanimous consent of the House I wish to propose a motion under Standing Order 43. The urgent and pressing necessity for this motion is explained by the following circumstances. I shall be brief, as Irishmen usually are on St. Patrick's Day.
On March 11 the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion announced in the House the areas that, effective April 1, 1970, will be designated as special areas. These initial designations will be effective to the 30th of June, 1972. Agreements are to be signed with the provinces effective on April 1. The im-21774-45
mediate projects under these agreements will involve commitments of $200 million and are to be started within the next few months. The precise boundaries of the special areas are to be specified in the agreements.
Sir, the only opportunity allowed for debate in this House so far has been the short replies allowed to spokesmen for the opposition parties when this statement was made. The minister, according to the roster system, was improperly absent from the House yesterday. The Standing Committee on Regional Development will not sit, it now appears, before the Easter adjournment. This important matter, therefore, cannot be considered in committee before April 1. Accordingly, since Your Honour has ruled that Standing Order 5 is obsolete and that a member does not have to attend the service of this House, with the resultant corollary that we have no assurance the minister will be available for the budget debate or, indeed, before April 1 or at all, I wish to move the following motion which is seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin):
That the statement of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion of March 11th on areas designated as special areas be referred to the Standing Committee on Regional Development: that the committee report back to the House thereon on or before Wednesday, 25th March; and that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion be ordered to appear before the committee during its sittings on the said statement.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. members of the NDP sought to minimize the dangers of inflation by saying that really inflation poses no dangers at all and that there is no danger of our pricing ourselves out of world markets. The financial critic of the NDP said copper prices had increased substantially, yet we still sell copper; nickel prices have increased, as indeed have the prices of all other raw materials, by a considerable percentage, yet we have no trouble in selling these commodities on the markets of the world. I most respectfully point out to the NDP through you, Mr. Speaker, that there is indeed a great danger, we shall price ourselves out of world markets if the terrible curse known as inflation is not stopped very shortly.
I ask my hon. friends to the left, is there not a danger of pricing ourselves out of the market for heavier machinery? Look at the Japanese steel that is invading our markets, even though we have some of the world's finest steel workers in Hamilton and other Canadian centres. Look at the competition in the automobile market. These Volkswagens we see running around come from Germany and our people are buying them because they are cheaper than other cars. Clearly, we are
March 17. 1970	COMMONS
pricing ourselves out of the world automobile market. That is why inflation must be stopped and that is why I agree with the government's policy relating to tight money. As a result of those policies there may be some unemployment in the country; bad though that may be for those who are unemployed, it would be even worse for the country if unemployment were to grow. If prices are allowed to go even higher and if inflation is not checked, unemployment will become greater. We shall not be able to sell our goods and services on the markets of the world or even in this country, because so many cheaper foreign imports will enter Canada. Also, we shall not be able to export.
Members of the opposition suggest the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has not done a good job in his budget because pensions for veterans and old people have not been increased. I think all members of the House wish pensions to be increased. We all know old age pensioners receive too little money. Most of us would like to double their pensions. Labour party socialist-

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I supported some of the rule changes, but not all. Those that were effective I believed in, and others I opposed. Two years ago I sounded a warning that if we accepted these rules we would actually destroy this institution. But members drank from the poisoned chalice that the government brought before them; they accepted it. On February 28, 1968 the Prime Minister said that the government, as long as it is the government, has the choice of deciding the manner in which it wishes to govern. Sir, no Prime Minister can exercise the right to determine the manner of governing without destroying this institution. These expressions, "participatory democracy", "just society" -does the House know who used them first? Mao; these are Mao's words.

I shall not mention any member, but some members have spoken out against the policy of being mere pawns who shall speak and not be heard. In 1956, this Parliament was over-run roughshod. In 1968, the Conservative Party accepted the large number of changes in the rules. It fought rule 16A, and finally 16A was withdrawn and the government obtained the other rule changes. Some thought I was wrong when I opposed many of these changes. As soon as the government was able to secure 16A what did the Prime Minister do? He made the statement that the trap was set and the opposition fell into it. That is not the way to treat Parliament. Then, a few months later, by action of closure, whatever rights remained to private members were virtually ended by the vote of members across the way who joined

in applying a halter to the head of Parliament. Sir, it is contempt of Parliament to act in this way. Parliament is not show business. I am amazed at the answers given to questions by members of this government. I admire the capacity to answer questions in both languages which the Prime Minister possesses, but how does he treat the members of this House? He snaps his fingers. Parliament deserves better than that.
Parliament has the right not to be given flippant and unworthy answers. Today, the Speaker of this House is tied by the rules. The question period has become ineffective and innocuous. Nothing controversial may be said by members sitting opposite the government-nothing argumentative. The new rules have paralysed this House. I shall not read from the British Hansard but, in summary, questions in the British House are placed on the order paper in writing and then supplementary questions begin. That is when the government is required to answer. Today, this government hides behind the rules, gives answers, and then when faced with a challenging question that question is out of order because, apparently, we have established rules which have the effect of rendering this institution innocuous. Is it any wonder there are few members present? I want to make clear that they did not leave after I started to speak today; they left before. I think of a Liberal leader in the United Kingdom. I shall not name him. They called him the "chamber-maid". Every time he got up he emptied the chamber. The Minister of Finance knows to whom I refer. The members are absent.
When this institution becomes a place in which there is no difference of opinion it will die. I am forced into the opinion that what is happening is that while the government gives to Parliament a kiss of approval it is a Judas kiss because it is placing this Parliament in a position where across the nation people say, "What do you do there"; "What is it". This is the institution that represents the freedom of you and me, sir, and every Canadian. It is being pushed down and down while at the same time the Prime Minister makes statements such as this statement he made on February 4:
I might add that as far as I am concerned it is true that I am going to establish a presidential system and this is why I always address you as Monsieur le President and not Monsieur l'Orateur.
The question period is totally ineffective. When the members of the government answer questions which they think they answered in

Sir, I would like to quote from that book: The Hatter opened his eyes very wide on hearing this; but all he said was "Why is a raven like a writing-desk?"
"Come, we shall have some fun now!" thought Alice. "I am glad they've begun asking riddles- I believe I can guess that," she added aloud.

All I have to do this afternoon is place before this House the danger to this institution. I have many more examples that can be given. Every member of this House is part of this institution. Every one is the inheritor of its freedom. Freedom has gone a long way in the field of human rights in the last six months by the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada in the case of Drybones vs. the Queen. This House now has greater responsibilities than ever before to not pass legislation containing sections, paragraphs or even lines constituting a denial of the fundamental freedoms provided for in the Bill of Eights.
All of us are creatures of this institution. It requires the dedication that was spoken of by Sir John Eliot who sat in the House of Commons under Charles I. Of him it was
March 17, 1970	COMMONS
said he loved his country, England, with a passionate enthusiasm which Pericles felt for Athens and he trusted the House of Commons as no one else.
Sir, you sit in the Chair that was referred to by the late Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King in 1921 in these words:
The constituent elements of Parliament here represented do right in regarding the present moment as one of historic significance.
That is when the Chair was delivered.
There are under British parliamentary institutions two symbols of authority-the Crown, which speaks of the sovereignty of loyalty, the speaker's Chair, which speaks of the sovereignty of the people. That, under the aegis of the British flag, those two sovereignties have blended into one is a tribute not less to the character and devotion to duty of the occupants of the British throne than to the genius of the British peoples in the art and science of government.
Tomorrow, in the other place, there is a conference to honour the former leaders of that place. Among them will be the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen who, on the same occasion said:
This chair will embody for us British traditions, it will remind us from day to day, through the stern trials of the future, of British wisdom and British patience. In Canada we are not all of one race; a large part are of French descent. But I shall echo and anticipate the words of those who in the ceremony of this afternoon will especially represent French Canadians, just so far as to say that they as well as we of Anglo-Saxon blood are attached to the free institutions that we inherit from old England, that they believe as firmly as we in the essential rightness and fitness of the form of government that she developed and that now is ours.
Sir, I did not want to say what I have said. I have sat here, I have listened, I have watched, I have felt. I have been deeply concerned and am now about what is happening to this institution, for if it goes, freedom goes. That is the reason I spoke as I did today, from the heart.

This program calls on the public sector of the economy to make all the sacrifices while it permits the private sector to go on its free and untrammelled way to make all the profits it can.
This proposal, Mr. Speaker, is one which the minister himself has admitted will mean

I anticipate some increase in unemployment. There will also be difficult wage negotiations. Some of these negotiations may issue in strikes-perhaps prolonged strikes-before settlements are reached.
My colleague, the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) was not exaggerating yesterday when he said that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) was urging employers to handcuff their employees, was urging employers to create situations by refusal to negotiate in good faith, to create tension and to have strikes. The minister knew what he was talking about, because unemployment is rising. The minister, of course, was not alone in talking tough. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in a press conference in December of last year said:
If people think we're going to lose our nerve, they should think again. We're not.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, it does not take much courage for the government to handcuff employees. It is not the cabinet ministers who are going to be unemployed or suffer as a result of inflation; it is the ordinary people, those who are least able to take the increased cost of living. It is those who will be unemployed who will suffer as a result of the kind of programs this government is proposing. The minister admitted himself that the program of restraint was failing to a large extent when he said in his budget speech:
There has been no slowing down in the rate of increase of prices and wages and other incomes. Costs continue to push prices up. Slower real growth has not yet reduced inflation.
There is no evidence and no belief by anybody except members of the government and a few of their tame so-called experts that this will happen. A commentator as sympathetic to the government as Anthony Westell, in discussing the minister's budget speech, reported in the Toronto Star of March 13, under a heading which I think is very apt, "Policies Will Cut Buying Power of Old and Poor", that the Minister of Finance said:
I'm not proposing any legislation on taxes or tariffs.
Mr. Westell comments:
But that's not the whole truth. His policies will in fact cut the purchasing power of the old, the unemployed and the other elements in the community too weak to defend their living standards.
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
For these unfortunate people-a million or more Canadians-Benson's figures and forecasts mean exactly the same as a tax increase.
Later he says:
But the number of unemployed will increase by up to 80,000 from the present 500,000. For these people and their families the budget forecast means a cut from a living wage to inadequate insurance.
In other words, Mr. Westell agrees with my suggestion that those who will suffer most under the proposed budget are those who can least afford to suffer. About half a million people are currently unemployed. The figures for January, 1970, show unemployment at 485,000 people, as compared with 468,000 in January, 1969. The unemployment rate for male workers in January, 1970, was at 7 per cent. Figures relating to young people show that the unemployment rate for those between the ages of 14 and 19 is 14.4 per cent. For those between 20 and 24 years old the unemployment rate is 8.1 per cent. These figures are disastrous. I find it amazing that a government headed by a Prime Minister, who comes from Quebec should embark on policies which are nothing but a bonus to the aspirations of Mr. Rene Levesque and his parti Quebecois. These people want an independent and separate Quebec.
The Prime Minister said that, if necessary, he is prepared to see unemployment in Canada reach a rate of 6 per cent in order to check the danger of inflation. What the Prime Minister obviously has not faced is that a 6 per cent level of unemployment for Canada as a whole means an unemployment rate of 8 per cent in Quebec, a rate which could increase to 9 or 10 per cent. All signals show that unemployment will become worse. Last year private investment in Quebec rose an estimated 3.5 per cent over the 1968 level, while capital investment in Ontario rose by more than 23 per cent. This means that unemployment, already serious in Quebec, will become even more serious. The young people of Quebec, those coming out of Quebec universities and technical schools, will not accept that rate of unemployment. What the government is doing is this: it is deliberately fostering unemployment, in order, supposedly, to hold in check galloping inflation. By increasing unemployment in Quebec, it is inviting the people of Quebec to express their resentment against federalism by voting for that party in Quebec which believes in a separate Quebec. These policies stem from the Prime Minister

March 17, 1970
who was elected to foster Canadian unity. During the last election campaign the Prime Minister said that there is but one Canada. Now, his policies will destroy one Canada.
We can see what is happening. Housing starts for January, 1970, as compared with January, 1969, are down by at least 25 per cent. If adjusted on an annual basis the housing starts for this January indicate that
158,000	homes will be built this year, whereas last year we built over 200,000 homes. This building slowdown means unemployment. We already see that there is less work. Automobile plants are closing for a week at a time. That can only mean a reduction in the purchases of steel, nickel and copper, and further unemployment or short time work in those resource industries.
The budget proposed by the Minister of Finance indicates the determination of the government, led by a Prime Minister who compaigned in the last federal election on the slogan of a "Just Society", to continue its policy of restraints in the government sector of the economy while, as I said earlier, not calling for any restraint on the part of the private sector of the economy. These policies have done nothing to stop or slow down the rate of increase in our cost of living. Figures released a few days ago show that living costs increased in one month by half a point. The increase in the cost of living last year was about 5 per cent. This increase, one of the largest in many years, has of course been felt most acutely by those on fixed incomes, the pensioners, the recipients of veterans allowances, mothers allowances and blind persons pensions, all of whom have had to bear with the 5 per cent increase in the cost of living. Old age pensions have been increased by just 2 per cent. All this has been happening at a time when the accounts of the Minister of Finance show a surplus of several hundred million dollars. The minister's name ought to be Scrooge.
I want for a few moments to deal with what I consider a deliberate, unscrupulous and unprincipled campaign that has been carried on by the government, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance with the active co-operation of the Governor of the Bank of Canada, the Deputy Minister of Finance and the Chairman of the Prices and Incomes Commission. The government and all these people have called for wage restraints. They have blamed the working people and labour unions of this country for

March 17, 1970	COMMONS
supposedly refusing to co-operate in the program of wage restraints which, it is argued, is crucial in stopping our current inflationary spiral. What the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and those high officials I have mentioned have not told the Canadian people is that salaries in the private sector and for the top civil servants, which include those people I have mentioned, have gone up substantially more in terms of percentages than the wages of the working people in Canada; that the incomes of self employed groups such as doctors, lawyers, engineers and architects have gone up very much more than the wages of workers, and that the profits of essential and key industries in Canada have gone up by astronomical amounts.
Let me illustrate the point. The Governor of the Bank of Canada, who has made a number of speeches about the need for restraint, was until recently receiving a salary of $50,000 a year. Within the last year, I think, that salary has been raised to $75,000 a year.
I presume, although the bank has kept very quiet about this, that the governor's pension entitlement will be increased correspondingly. There is not much restraint in that kind of salary increase. I do not say he is not worth the money; yet it shows little sense for a man who has received that kind of increase to lecture people receiving $4,000, $5,000 or $6,000 a year about the need for restraint.
The Deputy Minister of Finance was making $27,000 a year in 1966. He is now being paid $40,000 a year. That represents an increase of over 30 per cent in the last three years. I do not think any worker in Canada has been able to negotiate that kind of wage increase. Yet the Deputy Minister adds his voice to those calling for restraint. The Chairman of the Prices and Incomes Commission is paid a salary of $40,000 a year, probably twice as much as he was paid when he was a dean at the University of British Columbia. I am not suggesting it is too much money, but I am suggesting that workers oannot be expected to take seriously lectures about restraint from people who do not show restraint themselves.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
About ten days ago, the Chairman of the Prices and Incomes Commission made a speech in Saskatoon. I have not got the report in front of me, but I am sure I can paraphrase it accurately. He said that the whole policy of restraint would fail unless workers and their unions co-operate in the program. The same day his speech was reported in the
DEBATES	5123
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow Globe and Mail, a report prepared by H. V. Chapman and Associates Limited appeared in the financial section of that newspaper outlining what was happening to the salaries of executives. The article can be summarized as follows:
H. V. Chapman and Associates Ltd. reports the percentage of executives who earned more than $20,000 in salaries and bonuses rose by 9 percentage points to 40 per cent in 1969 from 31 per cent in 1968. The percentage rose by 8 points in 1966, 1967 and 1968 together.
The average increase in total remuneration was within a range of 10.1 per cent to 10.6 per cent, compared with 8 per cent in 1968, 7.9 per cent in 1967, 8.8 per cent in 1966 and 8.2 per cent in 1965.
That is what is happening to the salaries of executives in this country. Not a word has been said about this by the Chairman of the Prices and Incomes Commission, the Governor of the Bank of Canada, the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance, all of whom are quick to lecture other people about what they should be doing. The unions representing civil servants believe with good reason that, although the government has not publicly announced this policy, it has set guidelines of 5 per cent as the maximum increases which civil servants will be permitted to get from the government as a result of negotiations. That is substantially less than the top level civil servants have received. I suggest that if the Minister of Finance really believed in the just society the Prime Minister spoke about during the election campaign, he would apply the same justice to all civil servants and not just those close to the Prime Minister, cabinet ministers and other top level civil servants. The increases in salaries at the executive level do not just apply to those I mentioned.
The increases in profits by the large companies in Canada are astronomical. Similarly, the increases in their prices are astronomical. Last year we had a good deal of discussion about the price of copper. Some weeks ago the government was gleeful because they supposedly convinced the copper companies in Canada that they should reduce by several cents the proposed increase which they announced in the price of copper. What the government does not tell the people of Canada, and tries to hide, is the fact that in the 13 months, January 1, 1969 to February 1, 1970, the price of copper rose from 45 cents a pound to 59 cents a pound, an increase of over 30 per cent, even after the government put some slight restraints on the copper companies. Is it any wonder the workers in the
March 17, 1970


who can least afford it. It will result in decreased production. What I am saying has been said much better and by much more reputable sources than I. It was said in the last report of the Economic Council of Canada. Possibly because the Economic Council of Canada has been honest, has taken its independence seriously and has called the shots as it saw them, it is having difficulty in getting government approval to hire the kind and numbers of staff which it needs. Meanwhile, others such as the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras) in charge of housing and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) can get all the staff they need.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Let me read for the information of the Minister of Finance a couple of sentences from the sixth annual report published by the Economic Council in September, 1969. Note how correct they were in the light of what has happened since then.
Until some easing of price and cost increases takes place in the United States, Canadian policies to deal with domestic price and cost problems will be handicapped. Further fiscal and monetary restraint could conceivably simply result in higher rates of unemployment and economic slack with no more than marginal effects on current rates of increases in prices and costs. Moreover, tighter restraint in Canada this year is likely to have its main impact on the economy next year. And if excess demand pressures in the United States are brought under control by the latter part of 1969, the principal result of stringent demand policy restraints in Canada this year might well be seriously mistimed to push the economy into a poor economic performance.
The Minister of Finance ought to have listened to the Economic Council rather than to the Governor of the Bank of Canada or to his own deputy minister. What the Council predicted in September 1969 is happening in 1970.
In the few moments which are left to me, I want to return to the subject of the government's policy of restraint. Reports that the government has the active support of the business community need to be taken with a good deal of scepticism. The agreements made by the business community in those meetings with the Prices and Incomes Commission in February were full of loopholes. Price increases are continuing at an accelerating rate, profits are substantial; bank profits were never higher than they are today. It is not true, as has been reported, that all the provinces were in agreement with the government's policies. The submissions made by those governments disclose a great deal of
March 17. 1970	COMMONS
apprehension and disquiet. The provincial governments realise that they cannot hold the line; they realize that the services which they provide-schools, hospitals, roads, welfare and part of medical care-cannot be cut back and that the cost to the municipalities of providing essential services in an increasingly urban society will continue to spiral. They realize that municipal taxes in 1970 will increase as they have done in every year since the end of the war, and that in the absence of a reallocation of funds they will continue to be in a most difficult situation.
Let me quote from the submission made by the government of Manitoba to the conference of finance ministers held on February 16, 1970. Manitoba was faced by the insistence of the federal government that it co-operate in an attempt to persuade workers to accept a policy of restraint. If the latter cannot be persuaded, I suppose the next step will be to impose wage restraint, if not a wage freeze, upon the working people of this country. This is what the government of Manitoba said, and I commend this to the minister as a policy which he ought to have considered in the budget we are discussing:
Controls must be fair in their application. If wage and income controls are necessary, then controls on excessive profits are equally required. If the worker is to be restricted in his earnings, then profits must be equally restricted. If individual Canadians are to be denied wage or salary increases above certain levels, it is only plain justice-and common sense-that profits above given levels should be denied, by special taxation if necessary.
Compare that statement with the invitation extended to employers by the minister in his budget speech to be tough in negotiations with labour, an invitation which can mean only restriction-

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I am afraid his time has expired.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As
a rule, however good a minister of finance may be, however well he may be able to keep expenditures and revenues in balance, he can never expect praise from the opposition, not even in the unlikely event of his announcing substantial tax reductions. The budget which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) presented to the nation on Thursday is the first in 20 years which did not contain any major proposals for income tax changes, and the first in 57 years without changes in tariffs, in spite of requests, some for increases and some
DEBATES	5125
The Budget-Mr. Badanai for reductions. It is clearly an anti-inflationary budget, designed to curb the rise of consumer costs and to protect those on pensions and others living on fixed incomes. It offers a better approach to the future for the great majority of Canadians.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) could find nothing better to say than that is was "a cold-blooded effort", while the official Conservative spokesman, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) practically rested his case after describing the proposals as "cold turkey", whatever that is supposed to convey.
The budget contains measures to control the terms of consumer credit in order to reduce inflationary pressure resulting from over-spending. It provides authority to regulate the extension of credit to consumers by banks, finance companies, loan companies and other lenders. But it would not apply to credit in respect of small purchases, nor would the restrictions apply to loans for business purposes, including farming, or for loans for construction or to buy a house. Student loans for education would also be exempt.
An important feature announced by the minister was that the existing write-off of expenditures on water pollution control facilities will be extended to December 31, 1973. The cost of these efforts to control pollution will be written-off at a maximum rate of 50 per cent. These provisions will also apply to measures to curb air pollution, presumably by controlling fumes from automobiles and aircraft. The dangers from pollution have gripped the imagination of men everywhere. It is not only a national problem but one of international concern. Every level of government and our neighbours to the south must co-operate with both money and ideas in a total effort to control the menace which knows no boundaries.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Not all savings and restrictions are good. The government's drive to fight inflation by cutbacks in some departments is to be commended as an example to other levels of government of controlling excessive expenditures where savings will not impair essential services to the people. But the cutting of personnel in that section of the department of immigration which has to do with actual contact with prospective immigrants abroad, and the reduction of publicity to attract immigrants from Britain and
March 17, 1970

The Budget-Mr. Badanai Europe, do not merit commendation. In my view, this economy can only produce doubtful benefits to a country that is still an empty land when one considers the drop in the number of immigrants admitted to Canada during the past 15 months.
If the government wishes to correct the impression that its immigration policy is a cold and hot water tap turned on and off according to the direction of manpower winds, it has to revert to its more realistic policy of two years ago. I cannot help but feel that our present policy in immigration is one of timidity and inadequacy. We seem to have forgotten that the main goal of an immigration policy is to promote immigration to Canada of as many persons of good character as possible and to keep out the trouble makers. A modest figure would be 250,000 a year, but certainly not less than one per cent of our total population, irrespective of religion or ethnic origin. We should also assist to the maximum degree the reunion of families, with particular consideration being given to applicants sponsored by relatives and friends.
I have a high regard for our present minister of immigration, but I am not impressed by statements to the effect that the reason for the decline in the number of immigrants from Europe is solely the improved economic conditions in western Europe. The present points system is not working in the best interest of Canada. It is too restrictive in its application to unskilled workers. There is still a great demand for them in the fields of mining and agriculture, and in the construction industry. There are some people who are opposed to large scale immigration on the ground that the job market cannot sustain any major increases; but these same people have failed to back up their conviction with any documented facts to prove their contention.
It has been estimated that 30,000 new business ventures have been started in Canada by immigrants during the past 20 years, involving some $400 million in working capital and creating thousands of jobs, to say nothing of the valuable contribution these businesses have made to the sum total of Canada's development. Fortunately for Canada, we have a Prime Minister who thinks of Canadians as individuals, as people, not in terms of their ethnic origin; a Prime Minister who is concerned with the problem of cementing Canadian unity.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. D. Alkenbrack (Fronienac-Lennox and Addington):
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising at this time to make my small contribution to the budget debate I am reminded that this is
March 17. 1970	COMMONS
March 17, St. Patrick's day, a great day for the people of Irish ancestry. It seems to me, because of the ineffectual and mediocre nature of the budget, that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) in this Trudeau government is praying for a St. Patrick who would banish and expel all the serpentine troubles that are coiling and twisting around this government. These troubles will be the downfall of "Trudeaucracy". Most of the government's troubles are either of their own making or their own neglect.
What can I say about the budget? What can anyone say about it? It is barely worth a comment because it signifies nothing and does nothing for the Canadian people. Therefore, I believe we can call it a "ho-hum do-nothing" budget. It might have been part of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) and the Finance Minister's strategy to bring nothing forward at this time because in this same calendar year the Minister of Finance will attempt to perpetrate his notorious white paper upon the Canadian people. So, for the time being the Finance Minister says he is not proposing any legislation on taxes or tariffs.
Much as I should like to discuss the white paper during this budget debate, I shall not do so to any extent. I have other complaints of a vital and economic nature which I wish to make during the limited time I have the floor of the House. The Minister of Finance has said in his white paper that he will relieve many Canadians of the burden of paying income tax. That has merit. Why did he not begin to do that in this budget? I mentioned that he said he is not proposing any legislation in respect of tariffs. He said that possibly legislation will be needed by the autumn. Does he mean white paper legislation? The legislation in respect of his white paper proposals, if implemented, will mean the end of Canada as an influential, solvent, vigorous, manufacturing, land-owning and trading nation.
This Trudeau government, and the one before it under the Right Hon. Lester Pearson, have been creators of a man-made depression. The new Liberal concept of legislation, which now is a marriage made by that party with Marxist socialism, is sadly lacking. It lacks what it takes to govern a country like Canada. Here, we recall the strange anachronism of the Liberals in opposition in the winter of 1963 insistently clamouring about unemployment, at a time when there were
265,000	unemployed in Canada. I now refer to figures of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics
DEBATES	5129
The Budget-Mr. Alkenbrack for the week ending January 1970. These figures show that today, with the Liberals in power, there are over 485,000 unemployed, over 60,000 of whom are in Toronto. The Prime Minister, with a shrug of the shoulders and a gesture of his hand, says it is a calculated expectation and strategic fact of Liberal policy. There will be more unemployment. There will be unemployed Canadian farmers and bankrupt ones as well as a result of this government's former and present lack of policy and policy practices.
In the west during the past couple of years the Prime Minister has been saying, "Why should I be held responsible for selling your wheat". He did not hold himself responsible, nor did he sell any wheat. So, he now says, "I will give you money out of the public treasury to not grow any wheat and I will pay you at the rate of $6 an acre for those areas that you summerfallow and take out of production. It is quite a few years since I have worked on the farm in Richmond Township, Lennox County but the economics of farm operation still hold true. With the mechanized methods of today, one cannot summerfallow the wheatlands of the west nor the arable lands of any part of Canada for $6 an acre. I do not think that amount would pay for the gasoline or for the depreciation and the interest payments on the expensive machinery.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
However, enough of that, Mr. Speaker. We will leave the government wallowing like a wrecked and stranded tanker in the gulf of political bankruptcy and confusion. There are some things I want to say to the government regardinv their policies which affect the province of Ontario and my constituency of Fron-tenac-Lennox and Addington in particular. First of all, there are strong indications that this government is not looking after public works. The case in point is the construction of the Bath-Millhaven prison complex in my riding. For some time back we have heard that all is not well in relation to certain construction details of this prison and that there has been a lack of proper inspection by the Department of Public Works. I have in my hands a written complaint made to me by private individuals who doubt the soundness of the construction job being done by the general contractors, Argo Construction Limited and their various subcontractors. Here are some of the alleged discrepancies and divergencies from specifications. It reads as follows:
Building L. Footings are poured on top of granular fill not on bedrock according to specifications
March 17, 1970

The Budget-Mr. Alkenbrack and drawings. The 2" mud slab is to 2" thick, instead of 2" thick.
The 4" crawl space floor is 2" thick instead of 4" thick, which was authorized in the specification and drawings.
Buildings D, C and G. The south 40' of all these buildings bears the same construction defects as Building L.
Building F is the same. In all cases gravel has been used instead of going to bedrock.
Building S. The west half of the building crawl space has no reinforcing steel and this is contrary to specifications. The thickness of the concrete in all cases is not the thickness in the specifications and in all cases this occurs in crawl spaces where it cannot be seen unless investigated.
Kitchen Building. The east half of the crawl space floor is 50 per cent under the specifications both for mud slab and for the floor.
Guard Tower. The anchors that were supposed to go 5' into the bedrock were cut off with a torch. The concrete for this 40' high structure is poured on fill and not bedrock. The complete tunnel area is still visible sitting on top of stone fill instead of bedrock.
The above conditions, when considered present over millions of square feet of construction, would result in the savings of hundreds of thousands of dollars on the part of the contractor. J. L. Richards and Associates are the consultants. One B. Hilliard is reported to be the resident engineer who controls all the inspection and is paid by the government. Argo Construction is the general contractor for the Bath-Millhaven prison complex. I
I put this complaint on the record and hereby call upon the government to investigate it to the fullest with the object of correcting these alleged discrepancies. I have already placed on the Order Paper a private members notice of motion No. 393 calling for the tabling of copies of an inspector's report by the Minister of Public Works. Under the circumstances, I think that this should bring the government around to tabling and making that report public. The Bath-Millhaven prison complex will cost over $20 million and surely the Canadian people deserve value for their construction dollar in this case.
Another case where the government is not looking after business is the trade conditions arising from the wholesale adoption of the Kennedy round of tariffs under GATT. We find various Canadian industries reeling under the fierce international competition from low wage countries like Japan, Korea, Singapore and Hong Kong. This applies especially to the synthetic fibres industry in my area. Members of the House have seen what happened at Cornwall, the unemployment and hardship created there due to the invasion of Canadian markets by synthetic fibres coming from these low wage countries, and the total lack of interest in this problem by the Government.

I have received protests from the largest terylene plant in Canada, namely, Millhaven Fibres, situated in my riding and employing over 1,000 people. They are feeling the effects of this unfair competition. I have here a letter from Mr. Peter Humphreyes, resident manager of that plant, received today. I wish to quote parts of it as follows:
On October of 1968 the textile industry, both companies and unions, appeared before Prime Minister Trudeau and members of the cabinet to outline the major problems that imports from low cost countries were creating in the textile industry. They were assured that this problem would be dealt with soon.
Instead, a major re-examination of the situation surrounding the textile and clothing industries was decided on and the re-examination was to be completed by the end of 1969. The conclusions of this study have not as yet been revealed.
The major problems created by this repeated increase in imports is reflected in the fact that 20 per cent of all textiles and clothing in Canada now come from the low cost countries. Approximately 45 per cent of all textiles and clothing are imported into Canada so that the Canadian manufacturers are now supplying only 55 per cent of the Canadian market as compared to 70 per cent two years ago.
The increase in imports is not only having a disruptive effect on the textile industry in Canada, it is also having a disruptive effect of the livelihood of the 83,000 people who were in the textile and clothing industry in Canada.
Please note the phrase "who were in the textile and clothing industry in Canada,,< Many are still in it, but some are no longer there because of unemployment caused by foreign competition.
The letter continues:
We urge your consideration of an important industry which would be adversely affected in the future as far as continued operation is concerned. Consideration should also be given to the fact that this industry would be hard put to justify further capital expenditure to expand the economic climate of Canada without assurance that they would not be subjected to further increases in imports especially from the low cost countries.
Every member of the House will agree that in these cases, as well as in other industries in Canada, our industry must continue to have a certain amount of protection. This government joined the Kennedy round and GATT and thought they had done something big, but they walked away and left the door wide open. Our worst competition in synthetic fibres is coming from Korea. Their materials are being dumped on the Canadian market. I ask the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin): What do we dump in Korea? We do not enjoy any privileges there. 1 doubt if our exports to Korea amount to even one million dollars a year. I call upon
March 17, 1970	COMMONS
the government to take greater control of the situation and limit the dumping of these foreign synthetic fibres in this country in order that our own people can still hold their jobs and make a living here, which is their rightful heritage.
My last complaint for today pertains to the vicious escalation of tolls on the St. Lawrence Seaway and the Welland Canal, aided and abetted by the policies of the present and preceding Liberal governments. It is coincidental that the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) brought up the same subject. This was not prearranged and it shows the importance of this matter to Canadians. The escalation of tolls in the St. Lawrence Seaway is a bad thing, and this includes tolls exacted on the Welland Canal. We built the St. Lawrence Seaway in the last decade-that is the fifth decade of the century-at what is now a fairly nominal cost to Canadians of less than $340 million. What a bargain Canada got there! There should be no tolls on this waterway, and this is not the first time I have stood in this House and said so. I pointed this out four years ago, and yet there have been two increases in tolls since then.
The St. Lawrence Seaway system, including the Welland Canal, is at present the only stretch of commercially navigable water in North America which is subject to user charges in any form. Tolls on the St. Lawrence Seaway are no good for the economy of the heartland of Canada, namely, northern and southern Ontario. Not only do they increase the cost of all products manufactured by our industries, but seaway tolls are now beginning to increase the cost of our electric power, much of which is generated by thermal plants.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
On August 20th, 1963, I began to advocate a hydro generating plant in the riding that I represented at that time, namely, Prince Edward Lennox. I am now proud and pleased to see the beginning of the realization of that plant which will be built in South Fredericksburgh township in the county of Lennox, south of Napanee and west of Bath in the riding that I now represent, Frontenac-Lennox and Addington. We are now informed that this plant will be oil-fired and the oil will be supplied by marine transportation to the plant on the Bay of Quinte on the north shore of Lake Ontario. Neither the Ontario Hydro nor the manufacturing industries which will be using the power from this plant can afford to pay tolls on the oil and/or other fuels that the plant may use.
DEBATES	5131
The Budget-Mr. Alkenbrack
I have here a letter from Mr. Saul Laskin, the mayor of Thunder Bay, which I wish to put on the record as I think it is of vital interest to all Canadians. Mr. Laskin says:
Many people throughout Ontario believe that tolls on the international St. Lawrence Seaway and the all-Canadian Welland Ship Canal are matters of concern only to communities contiguous to those facilities.
But in a speech delivered before the Marine Club of Toronto on January 16, 1970, George E. Gathercole, LL.D., Chairman, Ontario Hydro, made it plain that such tolls should be of real concern to every user of electricity in this province- domestic, commercial or industrial.
As reported in the Globe and Mail on January 17, 1970, Dr. Gathercole in his statement made the following statements:
He expressed concern over the level of tolls levied on traffic in the Welland Canal and the St. Lawrence Seaway. The charge to coal shipped through the Welland Canal in 1969 was about $200,000.
While the figure is not high in relation to Hydro's total volume of merchandising, the Welland tolls are one of many pressures pushing the cost of electricity higher.
Mr. Gathercole referred to a statement in the report of the Great Lakes Waterways Development Association that indicated that increased tolls suggested by the federal Department of Transport could cost Hydro an additional $25 million for coal.
We would certainly oppose such an increase most strenuously and it should be clearly understood that additional tolls can only be met from one source-by the people of Ontario who use electricity.
I say, Mr. Speaker, including the people of Canada in general.
I thank Mayor Laskin of Thunder Bay for his letter and his support in the cause of the free passage of the commerce of our country on our great inland channel of contact with the whole world, the St. Lawrence Seaway. I and millions of Canadians look forward to the day when it will be free of tolls to legitimate shipping, as it ought to be.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Smith).

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the several members who have taken part in the budget debate for their excellent contributions. I was especially impressed by the remarks of the second last speaker, the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) and his remarks concerning friendship with our neighbours to the south. Mr. Speaker, you will not find much antiAmerican feeling in the maritimes, from where I come. Perhaps the reason is that there are more relatives of Maritimers in the New England states than there are Maritimers left in this country. I intend to be relatively brief and I think the hon. member who rose will have plenty of time to speak before the adjournment because I expect that my few remarks will not take more than 15 or 20 minutes.
In rising to speak in the budget debate, I would like to indicate my support of most of the budgetary measures proposed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) on Thursday last. I think all Canadians agree that fiscal restraint must still be exercised if inflation is to be brought under control and kept under control. A balanced budget was, therefore, expected and desired. Actually, the forecast is for a considerable surplus.
The surplus of the current year, as well as the forecast surplus, indicates to me good financial management by this government. The hardships that inflation inflicts on persons with fixed incomes is well known, and I need not elaborate on that. The serious effects of inflation on international trade is also well known. We must maintain our costs and prices at a level which will keep our exports competitive in foreign trade, a factor which is extremely important to the economy of this country as one of the large trading nations of the world.
One speaker yesterday, I believe the financial critic for the NDP, indicated that we are competitive in world markets regardless of restraint on costs or by labour. However, he cited such natural resource commodities as copper, steel or nickel. In nickel, for example, Canada has had almost a monopoly in the past. Recent and apparently major finds in Australia may change this situation considerably. As soon as the prices of our

products rise too high, a substitute will be found or, as in the case of nickel, other countries or companies in other countries, simply increase the intensity of their search so that they will inevitably make a discovery.
The restraint on government spending in the past year is to be commended. It is an example to industry and to the country as a whole. I believe the figures will show that the rate of increase in government spending was 3.8 per cent or less than the increase in the gross national product. This figure, of course, excludes the cost of joint programs with the provinces.
It is, however, unnecessary for me to cite the serious consequences of inflation. The effects are well known to all members of the House and by all Canadians. The proposals this budget contains were expected. As one newspaper put it, the condition of the patient, meaning the economy of Canada, was unchanged. In other words, inflation is not yet under control. No increases in taxation were expected in the budget and none were forthcoming. It is the next budget, or at least the main one for 1971-72 that will be awaited with great interest, and I might add, with considerable concern.
We in Atlantic Canada, Mr. Speaker, and in my riding of Northumberland-Miramichi have often complained that the government of Canada, in placing controls on the economy, has been unable to do so except on a national basis. In the Maritimes, where unemployment is chronically high-about 10 per cent in this season of the year-we suffer from these controls and restraints, while not contributing to the problem of inflation. As a measure to offset this, this government set up the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. I am pleased to note that substantial funds are provided in the present budget for this department.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Approximately $200 million is budgeted for the 1970-71 fiscal year. This department was promised during the last election campaign. We, in my riding, had great expectations of some swift action. I realize, Mr. Speaker, that the economic ills of the Maritimes which have prevailed for so long cannot be cured overnight. In the past, perhaps, moneys have been spent there that might have sparked industrial growth but sufficient planning had not been done and in some cases the money turned out to be largely wasted. So, I realize that research and planning in depth is
March 17. 1970

required. However, almost two years have now passed and, at least in my riding, no results are yet apparent. We are told that studies and planning are going on.
I am concerned about who in the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is doing the planning and what advice are they seeking and receiving. Are they seeking the advice of those who have wrestled with these problems for many years. I can say personally that no one has asked my advice nor, I think, the advice of any other member of Parliament. Perhaps our advice would be useless, but there is a chance that we might have something useful to contribute.
Any person who has held public office in New Brunswick has been greatly involved in trying to attract industry, because this is and has been our major problem for many years. Many Members of Parliament have been involved in the total economic problems of their province, town or riding for many years and know, or should know, something about the problems there. I do not discount the possibility of a fresh look with, possibly, new solutions being apparent to an outsider, if I may use the term, because as I say I have not been advised as to who was making studies, studies that are of intense interest to members. I do not know if these persons are students, college graduates or, in fact, if any have ever been in the Maritimes before. There are many maritime members whose advice might have been of some value. We have, for example, a member of this House who was Premier of New Brunswick for many years; another member is a former Attorney General of New Brunswick.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
Speaking personally, I was involved in the economic problems of my area as mayor of Newcastle, as President of the Board of Trade and as a businessman, for many years. We wrestled with the problem of how to attract industry. But we were always working without funds. Now that funds are available for this purpose through the Department of Regional Economic Expansion we, as members, so far as I know, were not consulted in any way or asked for any advice.
I am sorry to be somewhat critical of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) because he is not in the House today. On March 11 of this year, the minister announced the establishment of 22 special areas in eight provinces. Two of these are in 21774-47

The Budget-Mr. G. A. P. Smith New Brunswick, the areas of Saint John and Moncton. No one could quarrel with the need for special incentives in all or any part of New Brunswick. It was a disappointment to me, however, that none of the smaller centres which are most in need of help were designated. We had been led to believe that, in addition to the larger centres, there would be certain secondary growth centres designated as special areas. In fact, of the eight centres in Newfoundland-Labrador, six are to be in smaller communities. The others are at St. John's and Cornerbrook. My riding of Northumberland-Miramichi contains some of the lowest income and most economically depressed communities to be found anywhere in Canada. The designation of the towns of Newcastle and Chatham as a special area might well have attracted industry which would provide employment for members of the communities I have mentioned, and such a centre would, unlike Saint John and Moncton, be within a travelling distance for workers in the most depressed areas.
As mentioned by the minister in his statement of March 11, the special areas may receive assistance in providing an infrastructure of services which would be attractive to industry. The most important of these services in most cases will be transportation facilities. It was with pleasure that I read the announcement that the sum of $10 million is to be provided to start reconstruction of Highway No. 11 in eastern and northern New Brunswick which crosses my constituency. Another highway that should have high priority on any infrastructure of roads in New Brunswick is the one cutting across the central part of the province from Newcastle to Plaster Rock. This highway, now partly completed, if made an all weather road would open up the large central area of the province to which access has been very limited. It would connect the great potato farming counties of Madawaska and Victoria to the ports of the Miramichi.
However, the main transportation problem in my constituency, and one that we have been fighting to overcome for decades, is the lack of adequate water transportation. Our products are chiefly those from the pulpmills, sawmills and mines, and they are generally shipped to European markets, although some go to South American countries and the U.S.A. These industries suffer, as does our whole economy, from the refusal of the Department of Public Works to dredge an adequate channel to accommodate the larger ships that are mostly in use today. The ports of Newcastle
March 17, 1970

The Budget-Mr. G. A. P. Smith and Chatham are situated about 40 miles inland from the sea. The channel of the Mira-michi River is adequate, but there are one or two sand bars in the bay which prevent the entry of any but relatively small ships.
On many occasions over the years we have approached the Department of Public Works about this problem. I recall coming to Ottawa about ten years ago with a delegation to petition the then Minister of Public Works for improvements to the channel. Many delegations have since made the same request. The answer has always been in the negative. The negative reply has always been, "You show us the additional shipping and we will dredge your channel." Our argument has always been, "You provide the channel and we are sure the additional shipping will follow." In fact, we are now in grave danger even of losing the shipping we have enjoyed for several years. This is due to the trend towards the use of larger vessels.
I was perhaps able to accept this type of negative thinking from the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport. Now, the new Department of Regional Economic Expansion is expected to take a positive view in providing attractions to industry in the underdeveloped areas. It is supposed, in addition to financial incentives, to provide the facilities that industry would require.
Hoping for this positive approach to what I claim is our major problem in Northumber-land-Miramichi, another delegation from my constituency came to Ottawa almost as soon as this new department was organized. To date we have received the same old, negative reply. If the minister-I wish he were here today-is serious about providing a new approach, about providing an infrastructure of services, chiefly transportation, in the most depressed areas, I call on him in the strongest possible terms to take another look at this most pressing transportation deficiency in the only major port in eastern New Brunswick, that is, the dredging of the bottlenecks in the port of Miramichi-to a minimum depth of 26 feet.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
To return to the budget, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to note that in its attempts to combat inflation the government has realized that spending pressures have not been equally distributed across the country. The minister is to be congratulated for recommending the adoption of a measure that provides for higher


depreciation allowances on costs of commercial construction in regions of higher unemployment. He is also to be congratulated on his announcement concerning air and water pollution. The accelerated depreciation provision on devices, structures or equipment to reduce or prevent pollution is to be extended for a further three years: this is a welcome announcement. As the member for the constituency which embraces the greatest Atlantic salmon river in the world, namely, the Miramichi River, this was a most welcome inclusion in the budget. It remains to be seen, and watched with great care, that anti-pollution laws are strictly enforced.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for being so obliging as to recognize us in this far end of the House. I may say with all due respect that you are absolutely right in giving us the floor at this time.
I would first like to express my views on the budget speech in order to clarify certain points which, to my mind, are not clear enough and which too often cause useless discussions between the Ottawa government and some provincial administrations, particularly that of Quebec.
The main instance is the famous discussion on the $200 million that Quebec would like to recover while Ottawa intends to keep this income from the so-called social development tax of 2 per cent to use as it pleases, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has himself stated in the House.
Mr. Speaker, we must go back to 1939 to get a more comprehensive view of this matter. The then Premier, Hon. Adelard Godbout, had lent our taxation rights to Ottawa for the duration of the war, in view of the urgency of the situation. The war ended in 1945, and Maurice Duplessis, in his rather political statements, said that, for the sake of provincial autonomy, only certain taxation rights needed to be handed back to the provinces. Since the matter was profitable from a political standpoint, he did not demand that all the rights, transferred temporarily to Ottawa by Hon. Adelard Godbout, be returned too early to Quebec, so that he might thus cling to power.
Now, the Premier of Quebec, Mr. Jean-Jacques Bertrand, trained in the school of Hon. Maurice Duplessis who was defending that so-called autonomy, wishes to continue to beg for money that he claims is his own.
March 17, 1970

I feel there should be a round-table meeting in order to determine once and for all the tax jurisdictions of the federal and provincial governments. In the province of Quebec, the Creditistes have been improving the political awareness of Quebecers and in the last twelve years they have been successful in restoring the province's image through television programs. Soon, men of integrity will be elected to govern the province; their hands will not have been tied by electoral funds and they will have no financial curbs. They will proudly tell the whole population of Canada: Here is what we want to do. Let us stop our federal-provincial wranglings which, more often than not, are related to fiscal problems. What I have in mind, for instance, are the famous $200 million.
Here is, in my view, what should prevail in respect of this so-called social development tax. It seems to me that the central government should have frozen the $200 million until the Quebec government is in a position to accept hospital insurance. I suggest this course would have been more logical and the two governments would not have behaved like school children or immature adults. Canadians who are aware of this political verbiage say to themselves that we have not reached political maturity. French Canadians watch quietly this cock-fight that does not settle anything.
Mr. Speaker, in connection with existing problems in Canada, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has made a statement on a television program. Here is what has been said about it in a newspaper article entitled: "Mr. Benson agrees that an increase in unemployment is almost unavoidable", and I quote:
Perhaps it will be necessary to have an unemployment rate slightly higher than what it was in 1969 "if we want to check inflation", said Mr. Benson on television Sunday night.
o (5:40 p.m.)
Upon hearing statements like the one made by the minister, I become convinced that the problems will not be solved. In fact, to increase the unemployment rate is certainly not a step in the right direction. The time has come for all Canadians to work together in order to prevent such hardship amidst affluence.
In another article we read that 43 per cent of urban families are living in want.
Mr. Speaker, if the economic situation of 43 per cent of Canadian families is either one of want or one of hardship, I wonder why governments, federal and provincial, do not try to find a solution and do not stop 21774-47}
The Budget-Mr. Dumont dipping into the taxpayers' pockets. It should be decided whether it is the federal or the provincial government which should raise taxes. After all, the only problem with regard to the $200 million is to determine who has the right to collect them. Should taxes be levied by the federal or the provincial government? The first is too greedy; it imposes taxes and keeps all the money for itself. Hence all this ineffectual talk in Canada.
I maintain that the present government is not offering any positive solution. No problem is solved and instead of seeking complicated solutions it would have been better to put the Bank of Canada at the service of Canadians. Instead they have to pay taxes.
The saturation point has been reached long ago in Canada. Both in Ottawa and in Quebec no other solution was found than that of taxes and surtaxes.
In 1970, Canadians are not falling into steps. They are seeking another solution. Besides, we will be able to find that out on April 29. In Quebec we will see that the political education we have been spreading for 35 years now throughout the province will bear fruit. The surprise will be the miracle of the year. Overtaxed as we are, we do not accept any longer this financial system. Presently, without the permission of the capitalists who control the economy, even at the world level, and without leave from their servile officials in Ottawa, we cannot even breathe.
Therefore, we are against these taxes because, in my opinion, they are nothing but theft. They are theft, indeed, when they fall on taxpayers who have not enough money to buy the necessities of life, while goods are in abundance in this country. Taxes are theft when there are unsold products, when people are doomed to unemployment, when there is untapped productive power and especially when we note that it is impossible to sell products due to the lack of purchasing power.
In our day and age, taxes are a theft because they destroy the purchasing power, lead to an accumulation of products and deprive the population as much as inflation does. In my opinion, taxes should only exist to eliminate the excess of money in circulation when there are not enough products. When there is a lack of money, we do not need taxes but a redistribution of the purchasing power through the granting of a dividend or a compensated discount which would bring down prices to the real production cost.
I think there should be a different way of financing public investments, by the allocation
March 17. 1970

The Budget-Mr. Dumont of new credits according to the real needs and producing capacity of the country.
That is why the government's attitude is unacceptable. Indeed, even the Canadian Manufacturers Association maintain that Canadians will pay more for public services, since the government will draw an additional $500 million during the next five years out of the taxpayers' pockets.
The problem is thus to determine who will tax.
"It is patent theft", said the former president of the Canadian association of electrical appliances manufacturers, Mr. Ramsay.
"It is stupidity", said the president of the Montreal and Canadian Stock Exchanges, Mr. Charles Neapole. According to Mr. Neapole, the small Canadian companies will be the most affected by the proposed reforms as a result of the white paper and the new sources of taxation now proposed. As the matter stands, some companies like the Bombardier Co. of Quebec and other excellent Canadian companies will be affected, while others like General Motors which is controlled by American interests will benefit from the reforms suggested by the federal government.
For instance, in La Guadeloupe, in the Frontenac riding, where a snowmobile company was sold to an American corporation and overnight 300 workers were laid off. Attempts were made with the assistance of the union to find the owners of the industry and it was learned finally that they had fled abroad in a quiet hotel in Miami whose name was not known.
In the face of such shameless exploitation on the part of capitalists whom, in my opinion, take over our Canadian economy, it is time that the Bank of Canada be made to assist the Canadian people, so as to eliminate this economic system which interferes with our freedom and which binds us, although with golden chains.
Furthermore, we have been told that soon capital gains will be taxed. Let us not kid ourselves. We know fully well that it will be the consumers who will foot the bill. Prices will rise, which in turn will push upward the inflationary pressure. To operate and survive, a business must include in the price of the items it markets all its costs; otherwise, it faces bankruptcy. If one cost is not included in the price, the business loses money and eventually goes bankrupt.
It is impossible to tax effectively a capitalist producer, because his existence as a producer depends on his capacity or his ability to have

the consumer pay all the expenses generated by his business production.
Businesses will tend to inflate their prices according to additional taxes which the government will levy on them. It is impossible to believe that an unfair system will be improved with measures which will make it even more unfair.
With regard to capital gains on real estate, I submit that when we decide to appraise wealth in Canada, the home owner will be tempted to assess his property at the highest figure possible so as to protect himself or to minimize capital gains which could be obtained when selling his property later on.
However, if he puts a high price on his home, the chances are that the municipal appraisers will, in turn, step in and levy a higher land tax. There is thus no way of escaping from the recurring circle of problems.
On the other hand, if the home owner's appraisal is in keeping with the value set by the municipal appraisers, he will have to pay more taxes on capital gains than the profit he will make when he actually parts with his house.
In my opinion that is one of the ill effects of the white paper proposals. Mr. Fraser Robertson, in an editorial published in the November 12 issue of the Globe and Mail, notes the seeming disregard of the government for small businesses, because the white paper proposals result in discouraging small investors, in jeopardizing small businesses while favouring only the big monopolies.
According to this journalist, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) when bringing forward his proposals under the name of tax reform, obviously agrees with the view of the Economic Council of Canada to the effect that what Canada needs is to develop a few powerful monopolies likely to become the responsibility of other cabinet members. He knows complete disregard for small businesses.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Mr. Robertson adds that the disregard shown by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) for small business, more particularly the family-type businesses, reflects the arrogance peculiar to our times and our government.
Recalling that big businesses like General Motors and Massey-Ferguson had a modest start before becoming powerful monopolies, Mr. Robertson remarks that even in this era, big businesses are dependent on smaller businesses able to supply raw materials. He recalls
March 17, 1970

that General Electric, for instance, has to rely on more than 10,000 small suppliers.
Finally, without pondering on the Canadian situation for too long, I shall limit myself to a few examples showing that it is rather desperate. At the present time, there are in Canada two million children living in poverty;
350.000	women and 1 million children are on welfare. One urban family out of five earns less than $3,000 per year; the same goes for
160.000	rural families.
For these reasons, we Creditistes propose a minimum taxable income of $4,000 for married people, with a $1,000 deduction per child and a $2,000 deduction for single people. Moreover, the government should enact immediately a compensated discount so as to lower the cost of living and empower the Bank of Canada to make interest-free loans to municipalities, schools boards or for the establishment of any public service.
Moreover, so as to respect self-government and promote good understanding in Canada, each province should be granted, as was required by Alberta as soon as in 1935, the right to establish a branch of the Bank of Canada, so as to enable the provinces to finance, without interest, every public endeavour, thus promoting Canada's development while making financially feasible what is physically possible.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am happy to make a few modest remarks on the budget speech given last week by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson).
Through this budget, the government proposes various measures, various economic and financial programs to the House, in order to allow the members to put forth what criticism they see fit, provided it is objective, and serious, and that they ensure efficiency and dynamism in the administration of Canada.
The facts must be faced but, to my mind, it is a bad thing for criticism to be pessimistic only, and of such nature as to discourage the public. Occasionaly, it might be indicated for some of us to point out the weaknesses in a budget speech or in government programs. But, I do not approve of attempts being made to discourage the people by suggestions devoid of objectivity, useless suggestions that cannot help the Minister of Finance and the government to do even more efficiently the job they have done so well in the last few years.
What it amounts to is that we are asked to approve the government's general fiscal policy.

The Budget-Mr. G. LeBlanc We are not told to consider this policy as the most perfect one, as all members feel that any human organization is bound to have certain weaknesses, particularly when it comes to government policy and more especially as we work on what I might call human material.
And when we operate in this way it is difficult to use mathematical formulae entirely as they might be appropriate today but would probably have to be changed tomorrow due to the unpredictable evolution of all human activity.
The members of the opposition moved an amendment to criticize the government for failing to provide any tax relief for the poor and for taking measures to reduce consumer credit, which measures are likely to increase the difficulties facing Canadians and to increase the level of unemployment.
It must be acknowledged that these measures could be prejudicial to our workers for some time, but their purpose is to avoid a greater harm. In fact, it happens that the patient feels some pain when his doctor has to treat him for some disease. Another opposition party has also pointed out that the government should have considered the tax to be paid by single people whose annual income is under $2,000 and by married people whose annual income is under $4,000. In my opinion, the minister has already partly answered this question because it seems that after all these discussions we have had in these last few weeks about the white paper, which is not the statement of a final policy but a list of proposals, the small wage earners in Canada-as can be seen from the white paper-will be protected and that the strongest among the Canadian citizens, because noblesse oblige, will continue to hold the first place.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?
