speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I intend to use the few minutes that I have left to comment on the budget speech and to make some general observations as well as
5138	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. G. LeBlanc others concerning my riding in particular and the province of Quebec in general. I shall deal with those subjects within the framework of Canadian policy.
While listening to the comments of a few opposition members, I wondered whether some of them did not see in the budget speech some sort of speech from the throne.
In my opinion a budget is a kind of retrospective of the economic situation of the year just ended as well as an account of expenditure with regard to revenue so as to ascertain if the country is doing well or not. In the light of these facts, estimates are made for the year just beginning.
However, a speech from the throne cannot be compared with the introduction of a budget. In the speech from the throne legislative proposals are set forth. This seems simple but I think it is important to say it again so as to better identify the subject under consideration, to respect more our mandate, to fully avail ourselves of the rights and privileges given us by the people in order to safeguard the democratic freedom with the greatest respect and chiefly never to give the impression to the Canadian people that we are not getting anywhere and that the government aims only at bringing forward its policy as if it were the only remedy to economic problems.
It is always possible to find some weak spots in it and here is the proof of it. The government sets out its policy so that it should be commented upon. I bring that up again in order that the democratic image of our country should be a subject of pride for all the people of Canada. It is important that all the opposition members-they can be at times somewhat noisy since they take advantage of their rights-do not give the impression that they criticize the government policy only for the sake of saying that everything it does is not good and-which is more serious-forgetting meanwhile to make suggestions.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
All those who heard the Minister of Finance last week, have read the newspapers and discussed the highlights of the budget. The Canadian people generally and the hon. members in particular have them present in their mind. They deal with economic and financial conditions, with the needs of the government with regard to the development of Canada, so that we may co-operate for the welfare of Canadians.

DEBATES	March 17, 1970
Our sources of tax revenue, the allotment of public funds for next year, the federal statements of receipts and expenditures concerning public accounts and restrictions on consumer credit will soon, be the object of legislation, as indicated by the minister. Then all hon. members will be in a position to discuss the new policy on consumer credit as well as its effects, the various proposals concerning special accounts and loans, in the light of some precedents set in Canada and finally the problem which I consider as the most complex, that of differed amortization, and amortization of expenses incurred to fight pollution.
I would like to go over the most important aspects of the budget brought down last week, which gives all members of Parliament and all Canadians, of any political party, every reason to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and the government.
It is advisable and necessary to point out that taxes have not been raised for the first time in many years. The speaker who preceded me this afternoon, the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Dumont) discussed at length the bad effects of taxes in Canada, and he said that the government could govern without taxing. As he has been repeating for many years, he explained by what legerdemain he could replace taxes. But to my knowledge, there are very few countries, I should perhaps say there are none, that have used the legerdemain advocated by the hon. member for Frontenac.
A few days ago, the leader of his party, to whom I always listen with the utmost interest, was discussing provincial politics with a CJBR Station announcer in Rimouski and praising the merits of his party. To the people of my region he gave as a case in point the economic accomplishments of the two Social Credit governments in Canada, those of British Columbia and Alberta. To my knowledge, these two governments which are, if not the two most dynamic, at least the wealthiest, have not applied the policies of the Creditiste party. As a matter of fact, they are still using the coins and bills printed by the Royal Canadian Mint here in Ottawa close to Parliament Hill.
Why are those two provinces among the wealthiest, if not the wealthiest in Canada? I believe it is because British Columbia has a much milder climate than Quebec, which certainly affects the dynamic and efficient development of natural resources.
March 17, 1970

And Alberta, a pre-eminently agricultural province, has been developing for some years rich oil fields that may contribute to its prosperity.
For the first time, the budget does not provide for any tax increase. Maybe the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Dumont) would have been happy if there had been. For the first time also in many years, the budget shows a surplus, which is a sign of a sound financial administration and we should all be happy about it. The government has succeeded in attaining this object which was one of the priorities in its program during the election campagn of 1968.
For the first time again in years, the net amount of the national debt has been reduced. This is another point that we should take into account. In addition, we should keep in mind the efforts made by the government to maintain public expenditures within certain limits and to increase efficiency of public services, as well as in the administration through use of modern techniques, in the best interests of Canadians.
For years, opposition members have been claiming that the government establishes no priorities, as would be essential, whereas the government does have priorities. Since the beginning of the session, the government has been stressing priorities for expenditures, as can be ascertained by merely reading the budget speech made by the Minister of Finance.
In my opinion, highest priority goes to regional economic expansion, with a credits increase of $52 million. Next comes the program on behalf of Indians and Eskimos, with a credits increase of $34 million. In third place comes the retraining of manpower on which a credits increase of $24 million will be affected. Those who are afraid of unemployment can always take advantage of the manpower retraining program, so as to earn a decent living in a new trade.
We should not forget either the industrial and development incentives for which an increase of $12 million is provided. The government's appropriations for low-cost housing will amount to about $200 million. The government will provide an extra $15 million to help the have-not countries. The budget speech constantly emphasizes the war on poverty, first of all in Canada, and then in other countries.
And a last priority which has made the headlines in the newspapers and been the main topic of speeches given by politicians at
The Budget-Mr. G. LeBlanc all levels of government for some time is the fight against water and air pollution.
Some months ago, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) warned the Canadian people that if they failed to resort voluntarily to anti-inflationary means, the government, for its part, would take the necessary action.
Today, following the speech of the Minister of Finance, we realize that the government was serious, consistent and showing much intellectual honesty.
That is why we can proudly state-and again I say it-that the Minister of Finance, following such warnings, was the first in years to bring down not only a balanced budget but also one that showed a surplus. He clearly states that he intends to achieve the same thing in 1970-71. This is the reason why he managed to obtain a $250 million surplus.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the budget that we now have before us in the most clear and unequivocal fashion reveals the moral and intellectual bankruptcy of the Liberal Party of Canada.

speechtext:
The solution which that party presents to the people of Canada to the problems which our country faces is that we must in some paltry fashion tighten up consumer credit. If one reads the budget carefully, it will be seen that even in this nefarious enterprise only a half-hearted attempt has been made. Any serious economist would suggest that the recommendations in the budget to deal with consumption are not really effective. If the government wanted to put teeth into it, they could do what was done in this country in the early 1950's. Even operating under the assumption therefore that the economic problems of this country should be approached by reducing consumption, if we look at what the great old party on the government side of the House has proposed, we find a vacuous approach.
The budget is one more step in this government's neurotic two-year preoccupation with inflation which has not resulted in stable prices but in thousands of jobless persons throughout the country. The very important point that needs to be, and is recognized by anyone with a two-year university level of education in economics is that in a modern economy a government does have a choice. In fact, it has two choices. The economy can be geared so that society will be fully employed or, as I said a minute ago, there can be a neurotic preoccupation with price stability.
In the history of this country we have had governments which have consistently made the second choice. It is not necessary to rely on my partisan judgment for this: anyone can look at an economist's textbook on the history of economic practice in this country to make that discovery. I wish to quote from a source which at one time was very dear to the government. I am referring to Mr. John
[Mr. McGrath.)
DEBATES	March 17, 1970
Deutsch, the former head of the Economic Council of Canada. I shall read what Mr. Deutsch had to say about the deliberate attempts by governments of this country to manage the economy based on the assumption that what is needed most is price stability as opposed to full employment. In an article written in 1968, Mr. Deutsch, in comparing Canadian and American governments with their western European counterparts, pointed out that European governments
-have been highly sensitive to unemployment, and they have used monetary and fiscal policies very actively to keep the unemployment rates at low levels.
The result of this, he observed-and this is a deliberate policy on the part of western European countries-is as follows:
Over the past ten years ... they have generally succeeded in keeping the unemployment rate within a range of X to 2) per cent of the labour force.
He noted that in Sweden, in particular, unemployment in the past decade has rarely exceeded 1| per cent. During the same period unemployment in this country averaged about 5 per cent. I emphasize that this is a matter of deliberate government policy. Governments in this country have incessantly, foolishly and criminally opted for price stability over a fully employed economy. The increasingly evident result is unemployed Canadians. Canadians living in the Maritimes, Quebec, and now more and more in Ontario, the Prairie provinces and British Columbia are becoming unemployed. The recent figures are: the Atlantic provinces, 10 per cent; Quebec, 8 per cent; Ontario, 4.2 per cent; the Prairies, 4.6 per cent; British Columbia, 7.3 per cent.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
The atmosphere of unemployment is a disastrous one for people to grow up in, yet the most recent figures indicate that unemployment is now spreading to Ontario, the Prairies and British Columbia. This is a direct consequence of the policies this government has pursued for the past two years. The results are very evident in a constituency like my own where until the last couple of months we enjoyed full employment. Now, employment is beginning to decline. Automobile sales are declining. As an interesting sidelight, I might point out that imports of European automobiles have increased significantly during the last few months. Perhaps the chairman of the Prices and Incomes Commission should get in touch with those who run the auto-
March 17, 1970	COMMONS
motive industry and find out why they do not lower their prices.
One of the government's objectives is to bring about a reduction in prices, but anyone with an elementary knowledge of present-day economics knows that the big corporations are in a position to set their own prices; they are able to wait for decades, if necessary, before responding to the kind of fiscal and monetary policies which the government is operating. They dominate markets rather than respond to them.
Why is the government's deflationary program not working? It is obvious that it is not working, and I wish the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) had taken the advice of even some of his own economic advisers on this question. It is not working because current inflation is not caused by excessive demands on the economy. It is foolish to compare what is happening in the economy today with what happened in the fifties. In the early fifties there was, indeed, an excessive demand upon the economy; we were catching up in the production of consumer goods after the big lag during the second world war. The Korean war cut into the production of consumer goods. The labour force was fully employed, and too many dollars were chasing too few goods.
Today the situation is entirely different. There are plenty of goods waiting to be purchased, automobiles and manufactured products of all kinds. But they are not being bought. If hon. members will read what is contained in the sixth annual report of the Economic Council of Canada they will find that this is spelled out in detail.
My point is this. Though it is difficult to quantify these things, it is probable that 90 per cent of the inflation in this country is due to the inflation in the United States where it is the product of excessive demand. United States involvement in the war in Viet Nam has meant the diversion of a high percentage of its productive resources into military enterprises, leaving a gap in civilian production. In that country there are, indeed, too many dollars chasing too few goods. The United States is suffering from inflation, and we have inherited it in this country. I suppose the most practical early approach, the most realistic counsel to give this government would be to advise the United States to get out of the war in Southeast Asia. This would be the quickest approach to dealing with inflation in Canada. The result of the government's callous and outdated approach to a modern
DEBATES	5145
The Budget-Mr. Broadbent economy is bound to be even higher levels of unemployment, even more men, women and children suffering in a way which is altogether unacceptable.
One of the excuses put forward by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) is that if we did not take action to deal with inflation, Canadian exports would suffer. Once again, this is hogwash. Export figures for last month are up by 16 per cent as compared with a year ago; we have no problem in the export field. Besides, 70 per cent of our trade is with the United States, and the United States, as I pointed out a minute ago, is suffering from a higher rate of inflation than ours-theirs is running at about 6 per cent and ours is running at about 4.5 per cent. So we can expect to continue to trade with the United States in terms of the prices of our potential exports as long as inflation there is running ahead of our own.
What are we to conclude from the government's brilliant economic performance so far? The only conclusion I can reach is that they do not know what they are doing. They are following the old-fashioned conservative method of governing the economy, but even the application of this method is faulty because they have incorrectly diagnosed the present situation. This is the view of the Economic Council of Canada, as I pointed out a few moments ago.
What should be the economic objective of the federal government in this country? In my view it should be the same as that of every civilized country in western Europe: there should be a consistent, determined and intelligent approach to creating an economy in which there is full employment. Never, to my knowledge, has a government of this country presented us with a white paper on full employment, for example; it has always been on the subject of price stability, or something equivalent.
We in this party do not hold the view that inflation is something about which one should not be concerned. Of course, there is some concern. But we think in terms of priorities. The human priority, full employment, should come first. We must then be intellectually honest and admit that if there is to be full employment there must also be some measure of inflation. But let our primary aim be full employment, and then let measures be introduced to deal with the situation of those who-will be affected by the inevitable inflationary pressures accompanying it.
March 17, 1970

The Budget-Mr. Broadbent
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
Once again, there are no great mysteries about what ought to be done in this area. First, we should take measures to protect those on pensions, whether government or private. We need laws, applicable to private concerns as well as to government institutions, which will ensure pensions to people who have worked all their lives, based on income during the best ten years of their employment. They should contain escalation clauses which would correspond to the real increases in inflation, not to some arbitrary percentage level which is inevitably set lower than the actual rate. We need to protect people in receipt of pensions if we are to acknowledge that inflation will be with us in a full-employment economy.
The amendment we have put before the House would make some minimal move to provide relief for these people by raising tax exemptions from $1,000 to $2,000 for a single person and from $2,000 to $4,000 for a married couple. This would provide some real assistance to people confronted with inflation. Instead of providing this relief, the government has produced a nice white paper, in connection with which it is going to indulge in all kinds of extravagant propaganda for two years. It will then come along as the great beneficent father of the country and perhaps make a move in the direction which I have suggested.
I would ask the government why it does not make this move now. If, as the Economic Council of Canada has pointed out, these people are living in poverty, and I am tempted to say one hell of a lot of the rest of us are well off in this country, why not make a concession at this point instead of waiting another two years? We do not need to wait!
Another measure which would have to be taken to protect the people in an inflating economy relates to the barbarous trade union laws in this country. Something like a mere 40 per cent of our working force is unionized, a horrible shame in comparison with other industrial societies. For example, in Sweden some 90 per cent of the working force are members of trade unions: lawyers, doctors and other professions are proud to associate themselves with the labour movement and to be members of a union. This is something that we in this country must encourage. We must get virtually all our working people into a strong bargaining position so that they will be able to cope with price increases.


A third measure that could be taken is to unpeg the Canadian dollar. Because of our pegged dollar, whenever the United States economy is affected by inflation ours has to respond by making sure that our interest rates are just a little higher. In short, our economy has to respond to whatever the economy of the United States does. Therefore, one of the steps which would give us a little higher degree of independence would be to unpeg our dollar and conduct a vigorous, imaginative program to develop industries which are not directly dependent upon U.S. trade but would produce economic ties with other countries. These are four measures that a government of this country primarily concerned with full employment could take to protect those who experience difficult times as a result of the inevitable inflation that goes with full employment.
The final point I should like to make is that this budget fails entirely to encourage the development of the public sector of the economy. One of the most important methods of simultaneously protecting people against inflation and equalizing life opportunities for people in Canada is the provision of public or community goods and services. If we build public swimming pools, parks and universities, average and poor Canadians benefit as much as the rich. If we remove pollution from our water and air, preserve and build attractive cities, expand our hospitals, increase our medical research facilities and build at public expense more houses, on this economy we will have a substructure that will enable people to have real, human benefits at their disposal whether or not the economy is an inflated one.
This is extremely important. The more we rely upon market conditions to ensure production and distribution of goods and services, the more we put people in a very dependent position in terms of dealing with inflation. We must move much further in the direction of providing public goods and services so that people in society are not put in the position of having to compete in the marketplace for these goods and services. As a result, they would not suffer when confronted periodically with inflationary pressures.
I have made four or five suggestions about what could and should be done in this country of ours in a period of full employment when people are subjected to inflationary pressure. May I repeat that the government of this country has been an utter disaster from the point of view of economics.
March 17, 1970

It has been a complete and utter disaster when you consider that on a per capita basis we have one of the richest societies in the world. The government is still relying upon the most outmoded kind of thinking, and upon what should be the most outmoded moral position, in managing our society.
This budget should not be seen simply as a stand pat document which should more or less be accepted as one other document put out by a banal government. The budget should be seen and talked about for what it is-as the most current symbol of a government that does not know what it is doing and has no interest in changing the power structure of our economy, something that is necessary in order for Canadians to move toward a more civilized kind of existence.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I shall limit myself to the question of inflation and the so-called measures that have been taken by the government to control inflation. I fully realize that this problem is very serious and has to be faced. Like the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broad-bent), I say this is a problem that cannot be disregarded and that the measures which have been taken up to this time have been absolutely useless.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My good friend and colleague the Whip said recently I had apparently returned to normal. I should like to assure him that I have always been normal. Whenever reform measures are brought before the House which form part of Liberal philosophy, I support them. I supported the Criminal Code amendments and I now support the white paper which I think is a good social document. This is not the issue at stake. The issue at stake is that we as Canadians are bound to face inflation every five or six years. We are told it is about time to get down to physical flagellation in order to control inflation.
All these flagellists, including the minister, Mr. Rasminsky and all the experts, tell us we have sinned. What have we done, that we as Canadian people constantly deserve to be told that every five or six years we must restrict our economic enterprise and confine ourselves to lesser production? We are told not to grow crops and we are told not to do other things. This is not a country for negative thinking.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Negative thinking does not work. It may have worked 15 or 20 years ago but it does not work today. Let us consider some of the recommendations made by authorities as high up as Dr. Young, Mr. Rasminsky and

others. They say we must tighten money and we must restrict credit because this will have a beneficial effect on enterprise by making industry produce less. If these gentlemen were out in the commercial world they would realize that a restriction or a lessening of sales by any corporate enterprise is equivalent to automatic suicide because it results in a decrease in employment and production. There is only one result of decrease in sales, and that is bankruptcy.
These people still think businessmen should restrict themselves, confine their sales and produce less. This cannot be done. If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) had been out in the commercial world as I am from week to week, he would know this is not possible.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He would be getting $40 a week.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What is the consequence of this attitude? The banks, of course, have tightened up. They have said to the businessmen that they cannot have money because the banks are short. The businessmen know they must produce and increase sales, so they go to the friendly IAC-the Industrial Acceptance Corporation. That outfit says that this is a new and strange creature. They offer to help out businessmen by giving them money to purchase brand new equipment and machinery. They offer to factor their inventories at a charge of only 2 per cent per month. That is quite decent: if you calculate it for a year, it is only 22 per cent.
Then the manufacturers ask how they will dispose of their products. The finance company says not to worry because they will get customers. They in turn go to others and ask how they would like to buy these goods with money they will lend at only 18 per cent. I have in mind the entrepreneurs and the consumers, but the giants who get the profits are the finance companies. This all occurs because the minister says to the banks and finance companies that we must tighten up because we do not have the money.
I was a member of the Banking and Finance Committee when this situation occurred. This was the craziest snow job ever sold us as Members of Parliament. We were told we had to compete in the money market and that we must have a free interest rate in order to obtain investments in mortgages. How nice-the banks were going to invest all their money in mortgages in order that we might finance business enterprises and their inventories. We said fine, go ahead and finance these
March 17, 1970

companies in that way. Before we knew it, there were Chargex cards and Scotia Plan cards flying all over the place. We then found that was where the money at 38 per cent interest was going.
These banks which were originally vested with the right-almost a monopolistic right- in Canada to look after this service, we found to be derelict in this duty. There are two answers to the situation, and this does not involve instructing banks to restrict lending. If we are to give banks the monopolistic privilege of providing this money, which we have done, we must see that the interest rate is controlled, or insist that the money is placed where it is needed rather than where it can make the most profit. I have no objection to this, but the only other alternative is to throw banking wide open and get away from the branch banking system. Perhaps we should adopt the United States system of competitive banking. I have no objection to that, but in one way or another something has to be done.
The inflation illness which we suffer cannot be blamed on the working man or labour unions. It is due by and large to the fact that control of financing is left with the banks under a monopolistic system. Unemployment has been referred to time and time again. We must consider the consequences of unemployment today. The use of unemployment today, either directly or indirectly, as a tool to curb inflation cannot be tolerated.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Unemployment today has a much more serious consequence than it had 20 years ago. Unemployment today can no longer fit into protected groups. Today we belong to trade unions, and if one is a carpenter and is fired or laid off, his dignity is lost because he can do carpentry and nothing else. He loses his status and his earnings. This is a tragedy because the man who suffers from unemployment requires years to recover. He will never again be as productive as he might have been. The minister should carefully review his definition of unemployment in relation to how serious this situation can be.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
To say we may require 7 per cent or 8 per cent unemployment is just absolutely unbelievable. It is said that we are taking more out of the economy than we are putting into it. I believe that is true. That is the reason for inflation. We are talcing out more than we are putting in. The answer is not to take
The Budget-Mr. Otto out less; it is to put in more. Labour has no objection to this. Canadian labour today is about ninth in the world in productive capacity, after Italy and France. I believe it has a rating of 2 according to CNTU reports and DBS.
But what do we do with labour? First we say we do not really recognize unions; we say that a union is a quasi legal thing. Then we say you are still allowed to stop production and use the stoppage of work as a tool to negotiate, as if the negotiation was between labour and management. The fact is there is no management-labour dispute. Management will always pass on the cost. The dispute is labour-consumer or labour-labour. That is the conflict today.
It is about time this government put its mind to work and developed a system by which these disputes will be solved without a work stoppage. The consequence of a work stoppage is long-lasting. First, there is the lack of production. Heaven knows, we are short in production. Every year we lose out in respect of production because of work stoppages. When this happens, labour has to dip into its savings; it is no better off. Production suffers.
The most serious consequence is that if the labour dispute is settled over a long period, there is resentment; management and labour no longer see eye to eye; they are enemies instead of friends. There cannot be good production when there is that type of feeling. If this were 1930 I would say that there is no other method by which to solve a labour-management dispute, but this is 1970 and there are many ways in which it can be done. There is even the very simple method of abolishing unions and saying what firms shall be unionized. If there is no contract, the profits made during the period in which there is no contract could be turned over to the government. Management would have nothing to worry about because at least it would not have to close its factories or dig into its reserves. Labour would still be earning, we would still be producing and people would receive the benefit of this.
There might be thousands of other ways, but we should apply our minds to the essential question that so long as wages and prices increase at a more rapid rate than our gross national product, we will have inflation and it does not matter which economic philosophy is used. The budget indicated some controls over consumer loans. I grant that if any segment of our fiscal or economic policy has a great influence on inflation, it is the creation

March 17, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Otto of money because, indeed, consumer financing is the creation of money. Whether we think of it in direct or indirect terms, that is what it is. If you tell a man that he can buy goods and pay for them from his future earnings, you hypothecate his productivity and that is the creation of money. This has a great bearing on inflation. But to say that he must provide 20 per cent of the price and set a time limit for payment is of no consequence.
The finance companies promote the lending and borrowing of money. Your friendly HFC will lend you all the money you need in order to get out of debt. You do not have to pay interest on the debt but you do have to pay. They promote this. They are not worried too much. If a man cannot pay, they obtain a garnishee on his wages. The original law of bills of exchange and court procedures had to do with commercial borrowing, bills and bankruptcy; it had to do with people in business. They were in the commercial world and they were the ones who had to suffer the consequences of non-payment. It was never meant, and should not have been meant to be the tool of the finance companies to use to collect debts which they themselves promoted.
The solution is not in provincial hands; it is right here. All that we, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the government have to do is simply amend the Bills of Exchange Act and the Bankruptcy Act and say to the finance companies that if they promote the lending of money, they must collect it by promotion and be careful where they put it. They should make sure that the man is a good risk and not lend to him merely because he is a good fellow and then have recourse to garnishee proceedings. That might have some effect.
Let me in the few minutes remaining review some of the points I have made. Over a number of years we have had to tolerate less production from time to time so we might surmount the problem of inflation, but the problem has not been surmounted. We are now in the position of applying the same old remedy in the same old way even though it does not work. The essence of reform is to have a proper appreciation of the situation in order to find out what are the circumstances, and then apply measures and not just say we have measures which we are going to apply such as telling farmers not to grow crops and manufacturers not to produce. In essence, that is the reason for inflation.
In conclusion, as I say, I can imagine that some of these remedies would apply to many other countries. However, the statement that we import 90 per cent of our inflation from the United States does not stand up. If the United States is indeed involved in an expensive war, it obviously also can afford to be involved in lunar trips and expensive mineral exploration. A country which is hamstrung in respect of productivity could not afford to do this.
There is absolutely no need for Canada to be too seriously affected by United States inflation. I believe it is our own doing. It is up to our government to take a positive approach. It must say, first, that it will help business become more productive and will make money available to it at reasonable interest rates in order that business can improve its plant, it facilities and its production.
We should invite expertise in management and at the senior executive level from the United States or elsewhere so that Canadians can be trained to do a better job. The government should also come to a definite decision and policy in respect of labour. It is very nice to have our minister go from place to place in order to settle strikes, or to be there when they are settled-but that is not policy. We must have a policy in respect of what we want to do with labour and how we can make it more productive. We must remember at all times that the issue now is not that we should take less out of the economy, but that we should put more into it. We should enjoy the standard of living, with our productive capacity, to which we were entitled and not a standard of living dictated by restriction.

Mr. Speaker, in the couple of minutes that remain before the vote takes place I want to say that I agree in part with what was said by the previous speaker. One of the great problems facing this country at present is inflation.
My contention is that one of the greatest contributions to inflation at present is the high tax burden that Canadians are bearing. During the last 18 years the total tax burden on Canadians has risen from just over $6 billion to approximately $26 billion-a fourfold increase in a matter of 18 years. The most serious factor in this tax load and the

March 17, 1970	COMMONS
greatest single increase in the various forms of taxation has been hidden taxes. The result is that there is a tax factor in everything that Canadians buy.
There is now a sales tax at the federal level in most provinces, and some municipalities have a hidden sales tax in the price of everything that the Canadian consumer buys. The result is that there is an erosion in the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar to the extent that it is becoming more and more difficult for the average Canadian to bear his tax burden.
It is true that there are some Canadians who have a vested interest in inflation. Those who have real estate property of considerable value are in the position to ensure that the property increases in value. If they were fortunate enough to borrow money in the past to purchase that property, they can pay back the debt from the appreciation on the real estate property. More important still, the government itself has a vested interest in inflation.
I am convinced that they can never be completely convincing in their fight against inflation while this is the case, because as the years go by and inflation increases, the real value of tax exemptions which are set in constant dollars depreciates.
The result is that the tax load on Canadians automatically goes up without the government having to refer to Parliament to increase tax rates. In the last few years the government has been in a very satisfactory position so far as receipts are concerned and this government and its immediate predecessor-which was composed of the same people, shuffled about a bit-have been responsible since 1963 for what people have called the drunken sailor period of expenditures of the federal government.

I should like to say, Mr. Speaker, that it would be much easier for me to direct my statement to his statement had I seen it prior to the last minute and a half. I would say, sir, that the courtesy of this House surely would suggest, if not re-

quire, that spokesmen for opposition parties be apprised of documents of this kind before the last minute.
I would say to the right hon. Prime Minister that if he, in the face of a situation in Montreal which is crippling the mail service of this whole country and which is denying the people of Canada's largest city mail service week after week, can satisfy himself with such an innocuous document as he has designed to deliver to us tonight, his doctrine of participatory democracy has been left by the board long, long since.
I should like to know, sir, on this difficult day and yesterday when all these trials were upon us, why the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans)-who, surely to God, should have responsibility for these matters-has been silent. He did not present himself today to the Transport and Communications Committee at 9.30 and at 3.30. He did not present himself to this House today when he should have been available for questioning. I wonder why these people were not available for questions. I wonder how long the people of Canada should wait for mail service to be available for the people of Montreal and for the hundreds and thousands of Canadians whose mail service is dependent upon transit through Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, one of the distinguished and most literal members of the press gallery some days ago described the member for Hillsborough as being a Biblical character. Perhaps I am. Perhaps my appearance does that-

My friend says he smirks. When the people of Canada find it impossible to get their mail through the great distributing centre of Montreal, I say it is not a laughing matter. I would say, sir, that the measures which the Postmaster General threatened, then withdrew, indicate something less than a very appropriate or well-ordered minister of government. I would say, further, that when this government finds itself incapable of rendering to the people of Canada one of the most essential services, namely the delivery of mail to all the people of Canada, it should not be the object of smart aleck remarks by the Prime Minister and shrugs and smiles by the President of the Treasury Board.

subsubtopic: MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER OF INQUIRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the situation in Montreal with regard to the delivery of mail has developed into a national disaster. In Canada's largest city, a city containing 10 per cent of our population, for weeks parcel delivery has been at a virtual standstill. Although this disastrous situation has existed for several weeks, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) waited until 9.50 tonight before making the statement alluded to by my hon. friend for Hillsborough (Mr. Mac-quarrie). We had no opportunity to consider it until it was made. The statement says nothing. Why is there a crisis in Montreal? There is a crisis because the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) has ignored the advice of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey), the advice of members of the opposition and the advice of the arbitrator appointed to look into the dispute between the Post Office and its employees. The fact that there is that dispute ought to have warned the government that the Post Office today and for some years past had lacked personnel who understand the simple fundamentals of labour-management relations.

subsubtopic: MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER OF INQUIRY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
What is the dispute about? Very simply, it hinges around men who have worked anywhere from five years to 20 years delivering mail who feel that as a result of the decision of the Postmaster General to award, not one contract but five different contracts they will lose the jobs they have held for many years. Most of these men are too old to find new jobs. That, of course, is not something which would concern the Prime Minister. He has never had to worry about a job; neither has his colleague, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury). This is something that concerns others, Mr. Speaker, and what has happened has resulted from the Postmaster General's lack of understanding and his lack of compassion for those who will lose their jobs.
What does the Prime Minister propose in his statement? In this serious situation he proposes that Mr. Carl Goldenberg be appointed a commissioner to inquire into the problem. Mr. Goldenberg is an expert and has brought to a successful conclusion a number of important tasks of a similar nature to which he has been assigned in
[Mr. Speaker.)
years gone by. We all hope he will be as successful in settling this dispute as amicably and quickly as he has settled others in the past, and we wish him well. I submit that if the Prime Minister were concerned about settling the dispute between the Post Office Department and its employees justly and fairly, instead of appointing Mr. Goldenberg as arbitrator he would have asked for and received the resignation of the Postmaster General.

subsubtopic: MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER OF INQUIRY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER OF INQUIRY

Mr. Speaker, we see, in the light of the present situation, that the postal service is badly organized.
However, the government has taken action to meet a difficult situation. I think that was the right thing to do under the circumsances and it would be untimely to be critical of the postal service. We should rather wait for the investigator's findings.

1.	The ship to be drydocked for full condition survey by a steamship inspector; or, in lieu thereof, a detailed report to be produced of such a survey made since the ship was last in ice by a surveyor of Lloyd's Register of Shipping or of the American Bureau of Shipping, showing the hull, propellers and rudders to be in satisfactory condition and the ship to be still in class.
HULL:
2.	Ship to be in possession of valid Safety of Life at Sea and Load Line Convention Certificates.
3.	Hull of ship to be subdivided to give a one-compartment standard of subdivision.
4.	Hull to be reinforced for operation in ice and be fitted with an icebreaking bow and ice belt.
5.	Rudders to be strengthened and protected with ice horns for operation in ice.
6.	Still water bending stress in hull not to exceed four tons per square inch for all conditions of operation.
7.	Stress level of hull when breaking ice not to exceed the vessel's design stress.
8.	Quantity of fuel oil carried to be restricted to the bunkers required for the voyage of the ship and the supporting icebreaker.
9.	Where cargo tanks are used for the carriage of bunker fuel, only center-line tanks remote from the ship's side to be used.
MACHINERY:
10.	The ship to have sufficient propulsion power to operate in heavy ice conditions which shall in any case not be less than recommended by the latest published rules of Lloyd's Register of Shipping or the American Bureau of Shipping for
a vessel of its size classed for operation in ice. The astern power to be at least 35 per cent of the ahead power and be capable of being applied continuously for at least 20 minutes without overheating of the astern turbine.
11.	At least two boilers to be available for propulsion which are to be well secured to the ship's structure and provided with collision chocks of adequate strength to prevent movement of the boilers when the ship is brought to a stop from full power by ice. The steam pipes between the boilers and machinery to be supported in such a way that heavy shock and vibration may be absorbed without damage to the piping or machinery.
12.	Main machinery and essential auxiliary machinery to comply with the highest requirements of the latest published rules of Lloyd's Register of Shipping or the American Bureau of Shipping and shall be properly secured to withstand shock when navigating in heavy ice.
13.	Means to be provided for disconnecting either of the rudders in the event that one becomes damaged or inoperable and at least two independent sources of power to be available for the steering gear.
14.	The sea intakes and condenser inlets to be provided with steam or air lines, or other adequate means for removing any ice that may collect therein.
15.	A marked gate valve shall be fitted to the deck above each tank in which oil is carried. This valve to be in an accessible place so that a hose or pipe may be readily connected, and to have a diameter of at least six inches and may be fitted with a readily removable blank flange.

AND PERSONNEL:
16.	A complete set of up-to-date charts to be provided including charts of the largest scale available for the intended area of operation together with up-to-date pilot books, tide tables, lists of lights and sound signals, radio aids to marine navigation and similar nautical publications and associated ancillary equipment.

17.	The ship to be equipped with a gyro compass installation consisting of main and emergency gyros with steering repeaters at all steering positions and bearing repeaters suitably located and equipped, both gyros being suitable for high latitude operation and provided with spares and maintenance and operating manuals.
18.	A marine radar installation to be provided consisting of at least two radars which meet performance standards of the Safety of Life at Sea Convention 1960 and are suitable for operating under severe weather conditions. 19.	An echo sounder installation to be provided consisting of two echo sounders each having shallow and deep sounding capability. Both sets to be provided with

21.	Rudder, engine revolution and rate-of-turn indicators to be provided at the conning position.
22.	In addition to the normal radio communications facilities meeting international requirements and standards, VHF bridge to bridge radio telephone capability in the maritime mobile band to be provided.
23.	Auto pilot equipment, if used under difficult navigation conditions, to be capable of immediate manual override and a crew member assigned to steering duties to be at the steering position.
24.	An officer experienced in navigating in ice to be on board; and the crew to include personnel competent to maintain the navigation aids and equipment.
